Lim Guan Eng's Draft Manuscript (1965)
Document type/version: Draft manuscript (1965)

I completed this draft on 15 June 1965. It is not a finished work. I have left many pages with blank spaces where I hope to insert photographs and documents. I have also noted, in the margins, questions that I could not answer. Perhaps my children, or my nephews and nieces, will take up the task.

— Lim Guan Eng
15 June 1965

---

PART ONE: THE EARLIEST GENERATION

My great-grandfather, Lim Kian Huat, was born in 1858 in a village called Hou-shan, near Zhangzhou. The village is small, and I have not been able to find it on any modern map. My father said that his grandfather spoke of it as a place of terraced fields and a single stone bridge. Kian Huat was the second son. His elder brother stayed in China and inherited the family land. Kian Huat, having no land of his own, decided to try his luck in Nanyang.

He arrived in Singapore in 1883, at the age of twenty-five. He worked first as a coolie at the godowns along the Singapore River. Within a few years, he had saved enough to rent a small shophouse in Telok Ayer, where he sold rice and provisions. The business grew slowly. By 1895, he had bought the shophouse outright, and he sent for a bride from his home village.

His bride was Ng Ah Moy, born in 1865. She came to Singapore in 1896, and they were married in the Hokkien temple on Telok Ayer Street. I have a copy of their marriage certificate, which I will include in the appendix. They had four children:

1. Lim Soo Kim (son), born 1897
2. Lim Soo Lian (daughter), born 1899
3. Lim Soo Hock (son), born 1902
4. Lim Soo Choon (daughter), born 1905

Great-grandfather Kian Huat died in 1927, at the age of sixty-nine. He was buried in the Hokkien cemetery at Bukit Brown. I visited his grave last year with my father. The headstone is still legible, though the edges are worn. It reads: "Lim Kian Huat, born in the 8th year of Xianfeng, died in the 16th year of the Republic." My father pointed out that the dates correspond to 1858 and 1927.

Great-grandmother Ng Ah Moy died in 1942, during the Japanese occupation. She was seventy-seven. My mother remembers that she died quietly in her sleep, which was a mercy, as the times were hard. She is buried beside her husband at Bukit Brown.

Lim Chye Huat Family Manuscript first_draft_completed 1965-06-15 date. Record status: historical.

---

PART TWO: THE SECOND GENERATION

My grandfather, Lim Soo Kim, was the eldest son and inherited the shophouse and the business. He was born in 1897 and married my grandmother, Tan Swee Eng, in 1920. Tan Swee Eng was from Malacca, the daughter of a rubber dealer. I do not know much about her family, as she rarely spoke of them. She was a quiet woman, devoted to her children and to her kitchen.

Grandfather Lim Soo Kim expanded the business. He bought a second shophouse on Cross Street and began to trade in spices, especially pepper and nutmeg. He was successful, but he was also cautious. My father said that Grandfather never borrowed money, and he kept his accounts in a small black book that he carried with him everywhere. That book is lost, which is a great pity.

Grandfather and Grandmother had five children:

1. Lim Chye Huat (my father), born 1921
2. Lim Chye Lian (daughter), born 1923
3. Lim Chye Kim (son), born 1925
4. Lim Chye Hock (son), born 1928
5. Lim Chye Eng (daughter), born 1931

The family lived above the shophouse on Telok Ayer. My father remembered that the rooms were cramped, but the children were happy. The back lane was their playground, and the river was not far away. He told me that he and his brothers would sometimes skip school to watch the tongkangs unload their cargo.

Grandfather Lim Soo Kim died in 1945, shortly after the end of the war. He was forty-eight. The war had taken a toll on his health, and he had never fully recovered from a bout of malaria he caught in 1943. Grandmother Tan Swee Eng survived him by many years. She lived to see her grandchildren grow up, and she died in 1960, at the age of sixty-two.

---
My parents had four children:

1. Lim Guan Eng (me), born 1949
2. Lim Guan Chye (brother), born 1951
3. Lim Guan Hock (brother), born 1954
4. Lim Guan Lian (sister), born 1957

I was the eldest, and I was often given the responsibility of looking after my younger siblings. My father was strict with me, but he was also fair. He taught me to read and write in both English and Chinese, and he would often test me on my arithmetic. He said that a man who could not count his own money was a fool, and he did not want his son to be a fool.

My father continued to expand the business. In 1952, he bought a third shophouse on Cross Street, and he began to trade in dried goods, such as beans, mushrooms, and salted fish. He was careful with his money, like his father before him, and he would often say that the best way to grow wealth was to spend less than you earned. He was also generous to his employees, and he would give them a small bonus at Chinese New Year.

My father was a man of few words, but he was deeply devoted to his family. He would often sit in the evenings in the front room of the shophouse, reading the newspaper or writing in his ledger. He would not say much, but we all knew that he was watching over us. He died in 1965, on the 3rd of February, of a sudden illness. He was forty-three years old. His death was a great shock to the family, and I still miss him dearly.

---

PART THREE: THE THIRD GENERATION

I am the eldest son, and I have taken on the responsibility of continuing the family history. I was born in 1949, and I grew up in the shophouse on Cross Street. I attended the same school as my father, and I did well in my studies. After the war, my father sent me to the University of Malaya in Singapore, where I studied history. It was there that I became interested in the family's past, and I began to ask my father and my grandmother about their lives.

My grandmother, Tan Swee Eng, was a great source of stories. She would sit in the kitchen, shelling peas or grinding spices, and she would tell me about her childhood in Malacca. She remembered the rubber estates and the smell of the latex, and she would tell me about the floods that came every year, when the river would rise and cover the roads. She was a small woman, but she had a sharp memory, and she could recall the names and dates of relatives who had died before I was born.

My grandmother died in 1960, when I was eleven years old. I remember her funeral, which was held at the family home. There were many relatives, some of whom I had never met before. My father was very sad, and he told me that my grandmother had been the heart of the family. I did not fully understand this at the time, but I do now.

I began to write this manuscript in 1963, after I had finished my studies. I wanted to record the family history before the memories of the older generation were lost. I have relied on my own memories, as well as the stories told to me by my father, my grandmother, and my mother. I have also consulted whatever records I could find, such as birth certificates, marriage certificates, and old photographs.

The 1965 draft of the Lim Chye Huat Family Manuscript number_of_pages_in_1965_draft was 120 pages, and it is now complete. I have written it by hand, on lined paper, and I have numbered the pages sequentially. The draft is not a polished work; it is a collection of memories and notes, and I have made many corrections in pencil as I have gone along. Some of the marginal notes are questions to myself, such as "verify date" or "ask mother about this." I hope that one day, I or one of my descendants will be able to revise and expand this draft into a fuller history.
Page 97

**The Move to Singapore**

My father, Lim Chye Huat, was born in Malacca in 1898, the third son of Lim Boon Keng and his second wife, Ng Ai Lian. He grew up in a house on Jonker Street, which in those days was a busy thoroughfare lined with shophouses and small traders. The family had been in Malacca for several generations, and they were well known in the Hokkien community there. My grandfather, Lim Boon Keng, was a dealer in spices and dried goods, and he did a modest trade with the merchants who came up the Straits from Java and Sumatra.

The family's decision to move to Singapore was not made lightly. My grandfather had seen the trade in Malacca decline, as the port lost business to the newer and larger harbour in Singapore. Moreover, the British authorities in the Straits Settlements were encouraging migration to the new colony, and there were opportunities for those who were willing to work hard. My grandfather was also influenced by his brother, Lim Boon Tat, who had already moved to Singapore in 1899 and had set up a small shop on Cross Street in Chinatown.

In early 1903, my grandfather sold the family home in Malacca and arranged passage for the family to Singapore. The journey was made by sea, aboard a small steamer that plied the route between the two ports. The family travelled with their belongings, which were packed into wooden crates and canvas bags. My father, who was then five years old, remembered the journey well. He told me that the sea was rough for most of the voyage, and that his mother and the other women on board were seasick. The trip took about a day and a half, and they arrived in Singapore in the late afternoon.

The family initially settled in a shophouse on Smith Street, in the heart of Chinatown. The shophouse was narrow and dark, with a single room on the ground floor that served as a living and sleeping area, and a small kitchen at the back. There was no running water, and the family had to fetch water from a public standpipe on the street. My father remembered that the house was cramped, especially during the rainy season, when the washing could not be dried outside and had to be hung on lines inside the room.

My grandfather found work as a clerk with a trading firm, and my grandmother took in sewing to supplement the family income. The family was poor, but they were determined to make a new life for themselves. My father attended a Chinese school on Keong Saik Road, where he learned to read and write in both Mandarin and Hokkien. He also learned English, which he said was essential for anyone who wanted to get ahead in Singapore.

The family lived on Smith Street for about five years, and then moved to a larger house on Upper Nankin Street. This house had two rooms, and the family could spread out a little. My grandfather was doing better in his work, and he was able to send my father to an English school, where he did well. My father continued his education until he was about fifteen, and then he left school to work as an apprentice in a trading company.

Page 98

**The Early Years in Singapore**

My father often spoke about the early years in Singapore, and he had many stories about the people he met and the things he saw. He remembered the rickshaw pullers who crowded the streets, shouting for fares in a mixture of Hokkien, Cantonese, and Malay. He remembered the hawkers who sold noodles and satay from pushcarts, and the fortune tellers who set up their stalls on the five-foot ways. He remembered the Chinese opera performances that were held in the open air during the festivals, and the crowds that gathered to watch them.

My father also remembered the difficulties of those years. There was a cholera outbreak in 1905, and the family was very frightened. My grandfather insisted that everyone in the family drink only boiled water, and he forbade the children from eating any raw vegetables or fruit that had not been washed. My father said that he and his brothers were not allowed to play in the streets for several weeks, and that they spent most of their time indoors.
Page 99

**The Rubber Trade and South Bridge Road**

By the time my father was in his early twenties, the family had saved enough to think about going into business on their own. My grandfather had always been careful with money, and he had a good reputation among the merchants he dealt with. It was my father who first suggested the idea of trading in rubber. He had seen how the prices for rubber were rising, and he believed that there was a good future in it. My grandfather was hesitant at first, but he agreed to lend my father a portion of his savings to get started.

They set up a small shop along South Bridge Road, not far from where the family had first lived on Smith Street. The shop was narrow, with a counter at the front and shelves stacked with sacks of rubber sheets and blocks. My father kept the accounts in a thick ledger, and he would sit at a small desk at the back of the shop, writing with a steel nib pen that he dipped into a bottle of blue-black ink. My grandfather helped with the heavier work, hauling the sacks and dealing with the coolies who came to collect the rubber for the big European firms.

The rubber trade was not an easy business. Prices could go up and down from one week to the next, and there were many small traders who went bankrupt because they borrowed too much money to buy stock. My father was careful. He never bought more rubber than he could pay for, and he kept a portion of his profits aside for the lean months. He also made a point of learning the different grades of rubber, so that he could judge the quality of what he was buying. He said that this knowledge was worth more than money, because it allowed him to buy good rubber at a fair price and sell it to the larger firms who trusted his judgment.

Page 100

My father married my mother in 1915. The wedding was held at the shop, and the street was decorated with bunting and lanterns. My mother came from a family that had been in Singapore for two generations. Her father was a carpenter who made furniture for the European houses, and her mother ran a small provision shop in the same neighbourhood. My parents had known each other for several years, as their families moved in the same circles. I do not know the exact details of how they met, but my mother used to say that my father was always very serious, and that he would spend more time talking about rubber prices than about romance.

After the wedding, my mother came to live in the rooms above the shop. The rooms were small, but they were clean and well kept. My mother was a good housekeeper, and she kept the place neat and orderly. She also helped in the shop when my father was busy, weighing the rubber and writing out receipts for the customers. She was not afraid of hard work, and she often said that she preferred working in the shop to staying at home, because she liked to see the people coming and going.

My father’s business grew slowly. He began to deal with a few of the larger firms, and he was able to hire a young man to help with the deliveries. The young man was a cousin of my mother’s, a boy named Lim Cheng Hoe, who had come to Singapore from a village in Fujian. My father taught him the trade, and Cheng Hoe stayed with us for many years. He was a quiet, hardworking young man, and my father trusted him completely.

The shop on South Bridge Road was also a place where the family gathered. My grandfather would come by in the evenings to sit at the back of the shop and drink tea, and my father’s younger brothers would stop in to talk about their own affairs. My mother would bring down a pot of tea and some biscuits, and they would sit together until it was time to close. I remember these evenings very well, even though I was very young. The shop was lit by a single kerosene lamp, and the light would cast long shadows on the walls. The smell of rubber and tea and tobacco filled the air, and the sound of the traffic outside was a constant murmur.

PREFACE TO THE 1972 DRAFT

The present draft is the fourth complete revision of the family history that I began in 1963. The first three drafts were written for the private use of my immediate family. The 1965 draft, which was circulated to a small number of relatives, has been withdrawn from circulation, and I ask that any copies still in private hands be returned to me or destroyed. That draft contained a number of genealogical errors, particularly in the third generation, and its treatment of the Japanese occupation years was based on hearsay that I have since been unable to verify.

The 1972 draft incorporates three categories of new material. First, the oral history interviews conducted between 1970 and 1972 with surviving members of the fourth and fifth generations, as well as with two non-family informants who knew the family in the 1930s. Second, documentary evidence from the Registry of Deeds, the Singapore Land Office, and the archives of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. Third, a series of detailed comments and corrections supplied by Dr. Goh Cheng Teik of the University of Singapore, who read the 1969 draft at my request.

The manuscript now runs to 180 pages, including the genealogical charts and the appendices. This is a considerable expansion over the 1965 draft, which was 120 pages, and reflects the addition of the oral history material as well as the fuller documentation of property transactions in Chapter II.

By 1972, the Lim Chye Huat Family Manuscript number_of_pages_in_1972_draft had grown to 180 pages. Record status: historical.

I have kept the chapter structure of the 1969 draft, but I have rewritten Chapter IV almost entirely. The earlier version relied too heavily on a single informant, and Dr. Goh was right to point out that the narrative did not distinguish clearly between events that were personally witnessed and events that were reported to the informant by others. I have tried to correct this by attributing each recollection to a named source, with the date of the interview, in the footnotes.

A note on romanisation. I have used the romanisation of the family's own names as they appear in the English-language records of the period, rather than the pinyin forms that are now current. Thus "Lim Chye Huat" rather than "Lin Cai Fa," and "Neo Kim Lian" rather than "Liang Jin Lian." Where a person appears in a Malay or Dutch record under a different spelling, I have given the alternative in brackets at first mention.

I am grateful to Dr. Goh for his careful reading of the 1969 draft and for his letter of 22 July 1972, in which he discussed at length the question of how the new oral history material should be integrated. His suggestion that the interview transcripts be placed in a separate appendix, rather than quoted at length in the body of the text, has been followed. The reader who wishes to check a quotation will find the full transcript in Appendix C, keyed by interview number.

The genealogical charts in Appendix A have been redrawn. The 1969 charts contained a number of duplicate entries, and one line of descent was shown incorrectly. I have checked the present charts against the baptismal records of the Prinsep Street Presbyterian Church, the marriage registers of the Registrar of Births and Deaths, and the burial records of the Bukit Brown Cemetery, and I believe them to be accurate as of June 1972.

This draft is not yet in its final form. I expect that the Society's readers will find errors of detail, and I would be grateful for any corrections. I am particularly anxious to hear from anyone who can identify the photographer of the 1927 group photograph reproduced in Appendix B, or who can supply the name of the third child in that photograph, who is identified in the caption only as "Ah Seng."
The redrawn chart, which the reader will find as a folding plate inside the back cover of Appendix A, is arranged in five horizontal bands, one for each generation, with the earliest known ancestor at the top and the youngest generation at the bottom. The bands are not of equal height; the third generation, which is the largest, occupies nearly half of the sheet. I have kept the chart as a single sheet rather than dividing it into separate pages, because the Society's readers will, I think, wish to see the whole descent at a glance. The sheet is printed on heavy cartridge paper, and the folds have been placed so that the chart can be opened out fully without damaging the binding.

The five generations are as follows. The earliest known ancestor, Lim Pek Long, is placed in the first band. He is believed to have been born in the 1790s in the village of Khoo Heng, in the district of Changchow, Fukien. No record of his birth or death has been found, and the dates given for him in the chart are therefore placed in brackets. The second band contains his two sons, Lim Chye Huat and Lim Chye Kang, together with their respective wives. The third band contains the twelve children of Lim Chye Huat and his wife, Neo Kim Lian, and the four children of Lim Chye Kang and his wife, Tan Soon Neo. The fourth band contains the children of those sixteen third-generation persons, and the fifth band contains the youngest generation now living.

I should explain the convention used in the chart for the fifth band. Because the youngest generation is still growing, the chart shows only those children who were born before 31 December 1971. Children born in 1972 are not included, even where I know of their births, because the chart was checked against the baptismal and civil registers in June of this year, and I did not wish to enter names that I had not verified. The reader will therefore find that the fifth band is not complete. I have noted this on the face of the chart itself, in a small box beneath the title: "Fifth generation shown as at 31 Dec 1971."

For each person in the chart, the following information is given, where it is known: the full name, the dates of birth and death, the place of birth, the name of the spouse or spouses, and the date and place of marriage. For persons who died in infancy, the dates are given, but no spouse is entered. For persons who are still living, the death date is, of course, omitted, and the birth date is given without brackets. For persons whose birth date is uncertain, the date is given in brackets with a question mark, and a footnote refers the reader to the source of the estimate.

**Marriage Alliances and Their Significance**

Genealogical Chart of the Lim Family number_of_generations 5 generations. Record status: historical.

The chart records, in the columns to the right of each band, the marriage alliances of the family. These alliances are, I think, of considerable interest to the Society, because they show the family's connections with other Straits Chinese families of the same period. The marriages were not, so far as I can tell from the records, arranged with any deliberate policy of alliance. They appear rather to have followed the usual practice of the time, in which families of similar standing in the community intermarried, and the connections that resulted were a matter of course rather than of design. Nevertheless, the cumulative effect of these marriages was to bind the Lim family into a network of kinship with many of the leading families of the Straits Settlements.

The earliest marriage recorded in the chart is that of Lim Chye Huat to Neo Kim Lian, which took place in Penang in 1848. The marriage register of the Penang Registrar of Births and Deaths gives the date as 12 March 1848, and the witnesses as Lim Cheng Teik and Neo Ah Kow. This is the only marriage in the second generation for which a civil record has been found. The marriage of Lim Chye Kang to Tan Soon Neo is not recorded in the civil registers, and I have taken the date from a family memorandum which was shown to me by the late Lim Cheng Hoe of Malacca. The memorandum, which is in the possession of his grandson, gives the date as 1851, but I have not been able to verify it.
**Chapter VII: The Family and Education**

It is not possible to speak of the Lim family of Malacca and Penang without speaking of the schools they helped to build. The connection between the family and education was, in the first instance, a private matter. The sons of the house were taught at home by tutors, and the daughters, where they were taught at all, received instruction in reading and needlework within the household. The earliest record of such tuition in the family papers is a receipt, dated 1879, for the services of one Mr. Seah Cheng Watt, who was engaged for six months to instruct the children of Lim Chye Kang in the Chinese classics. The receipt is preserved in the family memorandum book, and it is the only document of its kind that has survived from that period.

The introduction of English education into the family came somewhat later. Lim Chye Huat, who had dealings with the firm of Guthrie and Company in Singapore, sent his eldest son, Lim Cheng Ghee, to the Raffles Institution in 1886. This was a decision of some consequence, for it set a pattern that the family was to follow for the next two generations. Of the eleven male children of the third generation who survived infancy, nine were sent to English schools, either the Raffles Institution in Singapore or the Penang Free School. The two who were not so sent were educated at home, one because he was delicate in health and the other because his mother, a lady of very traditional views, would not consent to his going so far from home. The latter case is worth noting, because it shows that the family's commitment to English education was not unanimous and that the older generation sometimes prevailed.

The first of the family to enter a profession was Lim Cheng Keat, the second son of Lim Chye Kang. He was admitted to the bar in 1898, having read law in London. The expenses of his education, which were considerable, were borne by his father and by his uncle, Lim Chye Huat, in equal shares. The family papers contain a letter from Lim Chye Huat to his brother, dated 10 June 1895, in which he writes:

*"I am glad that Keat has done well in his examinations. I enclose my draft for the sum of two hundred pounds, being my half share of the expenses for the coming year. I hope that he will justify our confidence in him. It is a great thing for the family that one of our name should enter the learned professions, and I trust that his example will encourage the younger ones."*

The letter is of interest not only for the light it throws on the family's financial arrangements but also for the value it places on professional attainment. The phrase "the learned professions" recurs in the family correspondence of this period, and it is clear that the family regarded the law and medicine as the highest callings to which a young man might aspire.

**The Founding of the Clan School**

The family's most substantial contribution to education, however, was not in the education of its own children but in the founding of a school for the children of the clan. The school was established in Malacca in 1921, and it bore the name of the Lim Clan Free School. The initiative for the school came from Lim Cheng Keng, the eldest son of Lim Chye Huat, who had returned from a visit to Amoy in 1919 with a strong impression of the schools that were being established there by overseas Chinese for the education of their poorer relatives. He proposed to his father and uncles that the family should do the same for the Lim clan in Malacca, and his proposal was accepted at a family council held in January 1920.

**The Family and the Raffles College**

The family's connection with education was not confined to the clan school. Several members of the family were active in the establishment of Raffles College in Singapore, which was founded in 1928. Lim Cheng Keng was a member of the college's first council, and he served in that capacity until his death in 1936.

**TRANSCRIPT EXCERPT — Tape T41, Side A (pp. 76–77)**

*The following is a transcript of the opening section of Side A, in which Madam Lee describes the ancestral tablets. The full transcript is in the blue folder marked "T41".*

**Interviewer:** Madam Lee, you mentioned last time that you would tell us about the ancestral tablets. Can you describe them for us?

**Madam Lee:** Yes, yes. They are in the hall, on the altar. The altar is a tall piece of wood, dark, very old. My husband's grandfather had it made, I think, or maybe his father. It is hard to say now. On the altar there are the tablets. They are made of wood, red with gold writing. The writing is very small, very neat. Each tablet has a name, and sometimes a date. The oldest one — the one at the back, the highest one — that is the one for the first ancestor, the one who came from China. His name is Lim Chye Seng. That is all we know. There is no date on that one. My husband said that the date was never written, or maybe it was lost. He said that when his grandfather was a boy, the tablet was already old. So we do not know when he was born, or when he died. We only know his name.

**Interviewer:** And the other tablets?

**Madam Lee:** The other tablets are for the ones who came after. There is one for my husband's grandfather, Lim Cheng Huat. That one has a date. He died in 1921, I think. And there is one for my husband's father, Lim Kim Seng. He died in 1948. And there is one for my husband's mother, too. Her name is on a separate tablet, next to his. That is the way it is done. The husband and the wife are together, but on separate tablets. And there is one for my husband's elder brother, Lim Kim Huat. He died young, in the war. He had no children, so my husband made a tablet for him, so that he would not be forgotten. My husband said that it is important that the name is kept, so that the spirit has a place.

**Interviewer:** And the rituals? Can you tell us about them?

**Madam Lee:** Yes. The most important one is Qingming. That is in April, usually, but the date changes every year. We go to the cemetery first, to the graves. We clean the graves, we pull the weeds, we sweep the stones. Then we put out the food. We bring tea, and rice, and sometimes a roast chicken. And we burn incense, and we burn paper money. My husband used to do all this. He knew exactly what to do, and in what order. Now my son does it, but I watch, and I tell him if he forgets something.

**Interviewer:** And the tablets, during Qingming?

**Madam Lee:** Ah, that is for the ones who are not in the cemetery. The tablets are for the ones whose graves we cannot visit, or the ones who do not have graves here. So on Qingming, after we come back from the cemetery, we also do a ceremony at the altar. We put out food in front of the tablets — small bowls, with rice and vegetables, and sometimes a piece of fruit. We light the incense, and we kneel, and we bow three times. Then we pour the tea into a small cup, and we let it sit for a while, so that the spirits can drink. After that, my son pours the tea into a little basin, and we wipe the tablets with a soft cloth. Not too much water, just enough to clean the dust. Then we put everything away.

S03/TR-14 — MADAM LEE KIM CHOO — SIDE A/B — 19 MARCH 1969

Side A runs about 22 minutes. Side B about 18. Recording is clear except for a stretch near the
middle of Side B where a lorry passed by and the voices drop. I have marked the transcript at that
point with a note. It happens just after she starts talking about her father-in-law's shop in
Tanjong Pagar, so the next few sentences are hard to hear. I have written in brackets what I think
she said, but it needs checking.

Madam Lee covers a lot of ground in this session. She goes back to the 1930s and talks about how
her own family, the Lees, came to Singapore from Malacca. Her grandfather was a tin miner in
Perak first, then came down to Singapore when the mines failed. She says the family name was
originally written with a different character, but her grandfather changed it when he registered
the children in school, because the teacher said the character was too complicated. She laughs
and says now nobody in the family can write the old one. I asked her if she remembered the old
character, and she said no, but her eldest cousin might. I have noted that as a follow-up.

She also talks about the house she grew up in, off Neil Road. It was a shophouse, two storeys,
with the family living upstairs and the ground floor rented to a tailor. She describes the
interior in good detail — the air-well, the wooden staircase, the way the light came in through
the roof tiles. She says the toilet was at the back, shared with the next house. The family had
five children, three boys and two girls, and she was the second girl. The boys slept in the front
room with the grandfather; the girls slept in the back with the mother. This is the kind of
detail that does not appear in any written record, so I have flagged it for the transcript.

There is a long section, maybe ten minutes, about food. She talks about what the family ate
during the war years, and how her mother would stretch a small amount of rice with sweet potato
and yam. She says the children were always hungry. She also remembers a particular dish her
mother made for New Year, a kind of steamed pudding with turnip and dried shrimp, and she
describes the exact method. I have noted in the transcript that she may be conflating two
different recipes, because she says the pudding had both turnip and taro, which I have not
seen together. But I am not going to press her on it. She is old, and the memory is happy.

The tape ends with her talking about her wedding, which was in 1941, just before the war. She
says she did not meet my husband's father until the day of the wedding, which is not unusual for
that time. She describes the procession, the red umbrella, the bridal chair. She says she was
fourteen. I have written her exact words in the transcript: "I was a child. I did not even know
what I was agreeing to." This is a strong statement, and I have kept it as she said it, but I
have also noted that she smiled when she said it, so I do not think it was bitter.

Follow-up items for Madam Lee:
- The old character for the family name. Ask if her cousin knows it.
- The recipe for the New Year pudding. Check if taro and turnip are both used, or if she
  misremembers.
- The date of her wedding. She said 1941, but she also said she was fourteen, which would put
  her birth in 1927. Her husband's family records show he was born in 1918. I have noted this
  discrepancy and will ask her again in the next session, gently.

documents.title: Lim Guan Eng's Draft Manuscript (1965)
documents.content:
I completed this draft on 15 June 1965. It is not a finished work. I have left many pages with blank spaces where I hope to insert photographs and documents. I have also noted, in the margins, questions that I could not answer. Perhaps my children, or my nephews and nieces, will take up the task.

— Lim Guan Eng
15 June 1965

---

PART ONE: THE EARLIEST GENERATION

My great-grandfather, Lim Kian Huat, was born in 1858 in a village called Hou-shan, near Zhangzhou. The village is small, and I have not been able to find it on any modern map. My father said that his grandfather spoke of it as a place of terraced fields and a single stone bridge. Kian Huat was the second son. His elder brother stayed in China and inherited the family land. Kian Huat, having no land of his own, decided to try his luck in Nanyang.

He arrived in Singapore in 1883, at the age of twenty-five. He worked first as a coolie at the godowns along the Singapore River. Within a few years, he had saved enough to rent a small shophouse in Telok Ayer, where he sold rice and provisions. The business grew slowly. By 1895, he had bought the shophouse outright, and he sent for a bride from his home village.

His bride was Ng Ah Moy, born in 1865. She came to Singapore in 1896, and they were married in the Hokkien temple on Telok Ayer Street. I have a copy of their marriage certificate, which I will include in the appendix. They had four children:

1. Lim Soo Kim (son), born 1897
2. Lim Soo Lian (daughter), born 1899
3. Lim Soo Hock (son), born 1902
4. Lim Soo Choon (daughter), born 1905

Great-grandfather Kian Huat died in 1927, at the age of sixty-nine. He was buried in the Hokkien cemetery at Bukit Brown. I visited his grave last year with my father. The headstone is still legible, though the edges are worn. It reads: "Lim Kian Huat, born in the 8th year of Xianfeng, died in the 16th year of the Republic." My father pointed out that the dates correspond to 1858 and 1927.

Great-grandmother Ng Ah Moy died in 1942, during the Japanese occupation. She was seventy-seven. My mother remembers that she died quietly in her sleep, which was a mercy, as the times were hard. She is buried beside her husband at Bukit Brown.

---

PART TWO: THE SECOND GENERATION

My grandfather, Lim Soo Kim, was the eldest son and inherited the shophouse and the business. He was born in 1897 and married my grandmother, Tan Swee Eng, in 1920. Tan Swee Eng was from Malacca, the daughter of a rubber dealer. I do not know much about her family, as she rarely spoke of them. She was a quiet woman, devoted to her children and to her kitchen.

Grandfather Lim Soo Kim expanded the business. He bought a second shophouse on Cross Street and began to trade in spices, especially pepper and nutmeg. He was successful, but he was also cautious. My father said that Grandfather never borrowed money, and he kept his accounts in a small black book that he carried with him everywhere. That book is lost, which is a great pity.

Grandfather and Grandmother had five children:

1. Lim Chye Huat (my father), born 1921
2. Lim Chye Lian (daughter), born 1923
3. Lim Chye Kim (son), born 1925
4. Lim Chye Hock (son), born 1928
5. Lim Chye Eng (daughter), born 1931

The family lived above the shophouse on Telok Ayer. My father remembered that the rooms were cramped, but the children were happy. The back lane was their playground, and the river was not far away. He told me that he and his brothers would sometimes skip school to watch the tongkangs unload their cargo.

Grandfather Lim Soo Kim died in 1945, shortly after the end of the war. He was forty-eight. The war had taken a toll on his health, and he had never fully recovered from a bout of malaria he caught in 1943. Grandmother Tan Swee Eng survived him by many years. She lived to see her grandchildren grow up, and she died in 1960, at the age of sixty-two.

documents.content:
My parents had four children:

1. Lim Guan Eng (me), born 1949
2. Lim Guan Chye (brother), born 1951
3. Lim Guan Hock (brother), born 1954
4. Lim Guan Lian (sister), born 1957

I was the eldest, and I was often given the responsibility of looking after my younger siblings. My father was strict with me, but he was also fair. He taught me to read and write in both English and Chinese, and he would often test me on my arithmetic. He said that a man who could not count his own money was a fool, and he did not want his son to be a fool.

My father continued to expand the business. In 1952, he bought a third shophouse on Cross Street, and he began to trade in dried goods, such as beans, mushrooms, and salted fish. He was careful with his money, like his father before him, and he would often say that the best way to grow wealth was to spend less than you earned. He was also generous to his employees, and he would give them a small bonus at Chinese New Year.

My father was a man of few words, but he was deeply devoted to his family. He would often sit in the evenings in the front room of the shophouse, reading the newspaper or writing in his ledger. He would not say much, but we all knew that he was watching over us. He died in 1965, on the 3rd of February, of a sudden illness. He was forty-three years old. His death was a great shock to the family, and I still miss him dearly.

---

PART THREE: THE THIRD GENERATION

I am the eldest son, and I have taken on the responsibility of continuing the family history. I was born in 1949, and I grew up in the shophouse on Cross Street. I attended the same school as my father, and I did well in my studies. After the war, my father sent me to the University of Malaya in Singapore, where I studied history. It was there that I became interested in the family's past, and I began to ask my father and my grandmother about their lives.

My grandmother, Tan Swee Eng, was a great source of stories. She would sit in the kitchen, shelling peas or grinding spices, and she would tell me about her childhood in Malacca. She remembered the rubber estates and the smell of the latex, and she would tell me about the floods that came every year, when the river would rise and cover the roads. She was a small woman, but she had a sharp memory, and she could recall the names and dates of relatives who had died before I was born.

My grandmother died in 1960, when I was eleven years old. I remember her funeral, which was held at the family home. There were many relatives, some of whom I had never met before. My father was very sad, and he told me that my grandmother had been the heart of the family. I did not fully understand this at the time, but I do now.

I began to write this manuscript in 1963, after I had finished my studies. I wanted to record the family history before the memories of the older generation were lost. I have relied on my own memories, as well as the stories told to me by my father, my grandmother, and my mother. I have also consulted whatever records I could find, such as birth certificates, marriage certificates, and old photographs.

The 1965 draft of the Lim Chye Huat Family Manuscript number_of_pages_in_1965_draft was 120 pages, and it is now complete. I have written it by hand, on lined paper, and I have numbered the pages sequentially. The draft is not a polished work; it is a collection of memories and notes, and I have made many corrections in pencil as I have gone along. Some of the marginal notes are questions to myself, such as "verify date" or "ask mother about this." I hope that one day, I or one of my descendants will be able to revise and expand this draft into a fuller history.

**The Move to Singapore**

My father, Lim Chye Huat, was born in Malacca in 1898, the third son of Lim Boon Keng and his second wife, Ng Ai Lian. He grew up in a house on Jonker Street, which in those days was a busy thoroughfare lined with shophouses and small traders. The family had been in Malacca for several generations, and they were well known in the Hokkien community there. My grandfather, Lim Boon Keng, was a dealer in spices and dried goods, and he did a modest trade with the merchants who came up the Straits from Java and Sumatra.

The family's decision to move to Singapore was not made lightly. My grandfather had seen the trade in Malacca decline, as the port lost business to the newer and larger harbour in Singapore. Moreover, the British authorities in the Straits Settlements were encouraging migration to the new colony, and there were opportunities for those who were willing to work hard. My grandfather was also influenced by his brother, Lim Boon Tat, who had already moved to Singapore in 1899 and had set up a small shop on Cross Street in Chinatown.

In early 1903, my grandfather sold the family home in Malacca and arranged passage for the family to Singapore. The journey was made by sea, aboard a small steamer that plied the route between the two ports. The family travelled with their belongings, which were packed into wooden crates and canvas bags. My father, who was then five years old, remembered the journey well. He told me that the sea was rough for most of the voyage, and that his mother and the other women on board were seasick. The trip took about a day and a half, and they arrived in Singapore in the late afternoon.

The family initially settled in a shophouse on Smith Street, in the heart of Chinatown. The shophouse was narrow and dark, with a single room on the ground floor that served as a living and sleeping area, and a small kitchen at the back. There was no running water, and the family had to fetch water from a public standpipe on the street. My father remembered that the house was cramped, especially during the rainy season, when the washing could not be dried outside and had to be hung on lines inside the room.

My grandfather found work as a clerk with a trading firm, and my grandmother took in sewing to supplement the family income. The family was poor, but they were determined to make a new life for themselves. My father attended a Chinese school on Keong Saik Road, where he learned to read and write in both Mandarin and Hokkien. He also learned English, which he said was essential for anyone who wanted to get ahead in Singapore.

The family lived on Smith Street for about five years, and then moved to a larger house on Upper Nankin Street. This house had two rooms, and the family could spread out a little. My grandfather was doing better in his work, and he was able to send my father to an English school, where he did well. My father continued his education until he was about fifteen, and then he left school to work as an apprentice in a trading company.

Page 98

**The Early Years in Singapore**

My father often spoke about the early years in Singapore, and he had many stories about the people he met and the things he saw. He remembered the rickshaw pullers who crowded the streets, shouting for fares in a mixture of Hokkien, Cantonese, and Malay. He remembered the hawkers who sold noodles and satay from pushcarts, and the fortune tellers who set up their stalls on the five-foot ways. He remembered the Chinese opera performances that were held in the open air during the festivals, and the crowds that gathered to watch them.

My father also remembered the difficulties of those years. There was a cholera outbreak in 1905, and the family was very frightened. My grandfather insisted that everyone in the family drink only boiled water, and he forbade the children from eating any raw vegetables or fruit that had not been washed. My father said that he and his brothers were not allowed to play in the streets for several weeks, and that they spent most of their time indoors.

documents.content:
Page 99

**The Rubber Trade and South Bridge Road**

By the time my father was in his early twenties, the family had saved enough to think about going into business on their own. My grandfather had always been careful with money, and he had a good reputation among the merchants he dealt with. It was my father who first suggested the idea of trading in rubber. He had seen how the prices for rubber were rising, and he believed that there was a good future in it. My grandfather was hesitant at first, but he agreed to lend my father a portion of his savings to get started.

They set up a small shop along South Bridge Road, not far from where the family had first lived on Smith Street. The shop was narrow, with a counter at the front and shelves stacked with sacks of rubber sheets and blocks. My father kept the accounts in a thick ledger, and he would sit at a small desk at the back of the shop, writing with a steel nib pen that he dipped into a bottle of blue-black ink. My grandfather helped with the heavier work, hauling the sacks and dealing with the coolies who came to collect the rubber for the big European firms.

The rubber trade was not an easy business. Prices could go up and down from one week to the next, and there were many small traders who went bankrupt because they borrowed too much money to buy stock. My father was careful. He never bought more rubber than he could pay for, and he kept a portion of his profits aside for the lean months. He also made a point of learning the different grades of rubber, so that he could judge the quality of what he was buying. He said that this knowledge was worth more than money, because it allowed him to buy good rubber at a fair price and sell it to the larger firms who trusted his judgment.

Page 100

My father married my mother in 1915. The wedding was held at the shop, and the street was decorated with bunting and lanterns. My mother came from a family that had been in Singapore for two generations. Her father was a carpenter who made furniture for the European houses, and her mother ran a small provision shop in the same neighbourhood. My parents had known each other for several years, as their families moved in the same circles. I do not know the exact details of how they met, but my mother used to say that my father was always very serious, and that he would spend more time talking about rubber prices than about romance.

After the wedding, my mother came to live in the rooms above the shop. The rooms were small, but they were clean and well kept. My mother was a good housekeeper, and she kept the place neat and orderly. She also helped in the shop when my father was busy, weighing the rubber and writing out receipts for the customers. She was not afraid of hard work, and she often said that she preferred working in the shop to staying at home, because she liked to see the people coming and going.

My father’s business grew slowly. He began to deal with a few of the larger firms, and he was able to hire a young man to help with the deliveries. The young man was a cousin of my mother’s, a boy named Lim Cheng Hoe, who had come to Singapore from a village in Fujian. My father taught him the trade, and Cheng Hoe stayed with us for many years. He was a quiet, hardworking young man, and my father trusted him completely.

The shop on South Bridge Road was also a place where the family gathered. My grandfather would come by in the evenings to sit at the back of the shop and drink tea, and my father’s younger brothers would stop in to talk about their own affairs. My mother would bring down a pot of tea and some biscuits, and they would sit together until it was time to close. I remember these evenings very well, even though I was very young. The shop was lit by a single kerosene lamp, and the light would cast long shadows on the walls. The smell of rubber and tea and tobacco filled the air, and the sound of the traffic outside was a constant murmur.

documents.content:
---

PREFACE TO THE 1972 DRAFT

The present draft is the fourth complete revision of the family history that I began in 1963. The first three drafts were written for the private use of my immediate family. The 1965 draft, which was circulated to a small number of relatives, has been withdrawn from circulation, and I ask that any copies still in private hands be returned to me or destroyed. That draft contained a number of genealogical errors, particularly in the third generation, and its treatment of the Japanese occupation years was based on hearsay that I have since been unable to verify.

The 1972 draft incorporates three categories of new material. First, the oral history interviews conducted between 1970 and 1972 with surviving members of the fourth and fifth generations, as well as with two non-family informants who knew the family in the 1930s. Second, documentary evidence from the Registry of Deeds, the Singapore Land Office, and the archives of the Chinese Chamber of Commerce. Third, a series of detailed comments and corrections supplied by Dr. Goh Cheng Teik of the University of Singapore, who read the 1969 draft at my request.

The manuscript now runs to 180 pages, including the genealogical charts and the appendices. This is a considerable expansion over the 1965 draft, which was 120 pages, and reflects the addition of the oral history material as well as the fuller documentation of property transactions in Chapter II.

By 1972, the Lim Chye Huat Family Manuscript number_of_pages_in_1972_draft had grown to 180 pages. Record status: historical.

I have kept the chapter structure of the 1969 draft, but I have rewritten Chapter IV almost entirely. The earlier version relied too heavily on a single informant, and Dr. Goh was right to point out that the narrative did not distinguish clearly between events that were personally witnessed and events that were reported to the informant by others. I have tried to correct this by attributing each recollection to a named source, with the date of the interview, in the footnotes.

A note on romanisation. I have used the romanisation of the family's own names as they appear in the English-language records of the period, rather than the pinyin forms that are now current. Thus "Lim Chye Huat" rather than "Lin Cai Fa," and "Neo Kim Lian" rather than "Liang Jin Lian." Where a person appears in a Malay or Dutch record under a different spelling, I have given the alternative in brackets at first mention.

I am grateful to Dr. Goh for his careful reading of the 1969 draft and for his letter of 22 July 1972, in which he discussed at length the question of how the new oral history material should be integrated. His suggestion that the interview transcripts be placed in a separate appendix, rather than quoted at length in the body of the text, has been followed. The reader who wishes to check a quotation will find the full transcript in Appendix C, keyed by interview number.

The genealogical charts in Appendix A have been redrawn. The 1969 charts contained a number of duplicate entries, and one line of descent was shown incorrectly. I have checked the present charts against the baptismal records of the Prinsep Street Presbyterian Church, the marriage registers of the Registrar of Births and Deaths, and the burial records of the Bukit Brown Cemetery, and I believe them to be accurate as of June 1972.

This draft is not yet in its final form. I expect that the Society's readers will find errors of detail, and I would be grateful for any corrections. I am particularly anxious to hear from anyone who can identify the photographer of the 1927 group photograph reproduced in Appendix B, or who can supply the name of the third child in that photograph, who is identified in the caption only as "Ah Seng."

documents.content:
The redrawn chart, which the reader will find as a folding plate inside the back cover of Appendix A, is arranged in five horizontal bands, one for each generation, with the earliest known ancestor at the top and the youngest generation at the bottom. The bands are not of equal height; the third generation, which is the largest, occupies nearly half of the sheet. I have kept the chart as a single sheet rather than dividing it into separate pages, because the Society's readers will, I think, wish to see the whole descent at a glance. The sheet is printed on heavy cartridge paper, and the folds have been placed so that the chart can be opened out fully without damaging the binding.

The five generations are as follows. The earliest known ancestor, Lim Pek Long, is placed in the first band. He is believed to have been born in the 1790s in the village of Khoo Heng, in the district of Changchow, Fukien. No record of his birth or death has been found, and the dates given for him in the chart are therefore placed in brackets. The second band contains his two sons, Lim Chye Huat and Lim Chye Kang, together with their respective wives. The third band contains the twelve children of Lim Chye Huat and his wife, Neo Kim Lian, and the four children of Lim Chye Kang and his wife, Tan Soon Neo. The fourth band contains the children of those sixteen third-generation persons, and the fifth band contains the youngest generation now living.

I should explain the convention used in the chart for the fifth band. Because the youngest generation is still growing, the chart shows only those children who were born before 31 December 1971. Children born in 1972 are not included, even where I know of their births, because the chart was checked against the baptismal and civil registers in June of this year, and I did not wish to enter names that I had not verified. The reader will therefore find that the fifth band is not complete. I have noted this on the face of the chart itself, in a small box beneath the title: "Fifth generation shown as at 31 Dec 1971."

For each person in the chart, the following information is given, where it is known: the full name, the dates of birth and death, the place of birth, the name of the spouse or spouses, and the date and place of marriage. For persons who died in infancy, the dates are given, but no spouse is entered. For persons who are still living, the death date is, of course, omitted, and the birth date is given without brackets. For persons whose birth date is uncertain, the date is given in brackets with a question mark, and a footnote refers the reader to the source of the estimate.

**Marriage Alliances and Their Significance**

Genealogical Chart of the Lim Family number_of_generations 5 generations. Record status: historical.

The chart records, in the columns to the right of each band, the marriage alliances of the family. These alliances are, I think, of considerable interest to the Society, because they show the family's connections with other Straits Chinese families of the same period. The marriages were not, so far as I can tell from the records, arranged with any deliberate policy of alliance. They appear rather to have followed the usual practice of the time, in which families of similar standing in the community intermarried, and the connections that resulted were a matter of course rather than of design. Nevertheless, the cumulative effect of these marriages was to bind the Lim family into a network of kinship with many of the leading families of the Straits Settlements.

The earliest marriage recorded in the chart is that of Lim Chye Huat to Neo Kim Lian, which took place in Penang in 1848. The marriage register of the Penang Registrar of Births and Deaths gives the date as 12 March 1848, and the witnesses as Lim Cheng Teik and Neo Ah Kow. This is the only marriage in the second generation for which a civil record has been found. The marriage of Lim Chye Kang to Tan Soon Neo is not recorded in the civil registers, and I have taken the date from a family memorandum which was shown to me by the late Lim Cheng Hoe of Malacca. The memorandum, which is in the possession of his grandson, gives the date as 1851, but I have not been able to verify it.

**Chapter VII: The Family and Education**

It is not possible to speak of the Lim family of Malacca and Penang without speaking of the schools they helped to build. The connection between the family and education was, in the first instance, a private matter. The sons of the house were taught at home by tutors, and the daughters, where they were taught at all, received instruction in reading and needlework within the household. The earliest record of such tuition in the family papers is a receipt, dated 1879, for the services of one Mr. Seah Cheng Watt, who was engaged for six months to instruct the children of Lim Chye Kang in the Chinese classics. The receipt is preserved in the family memorandum book, and it is the only document of its kind that has survived from that period.

The introduction of English education into the family came somewhat later. Lim Chye Huat, who had dealings with the firm of Guthrie and Company in Singapore, sent his eldest son, Lim Cheng Ghee, to the Raffles Institution in 1886. This was a decision of some consequence, for it set a pattern that the family was to follow for the next two generations. Of the eleven male children of the third generation who survived infancy, nine were sent to English schools, either the Raffles Institution in Singapore or the Penang Free School. The two who were not so sent were educated at home, one because he was delicate in health and the other because his mother, a lady of very traditional views, would not consent to his going so far from home. The latter case is worth noting, because it shows that the family's commitment to English education was not unanimous and that the older generation sometimes prevailed.

The first of the family to enter a profession was Lim Cheng Keat, the second son of Lim Chye Kang. He was admitted to the bar in 1898, having read law in London. The expenses of his education, which were considerable, were borne by his father and by his uncle, Lim Chye Huat, in equal shares. The family papers contain a letter from Lim Chye Huat to his brother, dated 10 June 1895, in which he writes:

*"I am glad that Keat has done well in his examinations. I enclose my draft for the sum of two hundred pounds, being my half share of the expenses for the coming year. I hope that he will justify our confidence in him. It is a great thing for the family that one of our name should enter the learned professions, and I trust that his example will encourage the younger ones."*

The letter is of interest not only for the light it throws on the family's financial arrangements but also for the value it places on professional attainment. The phrase "the learned professions" recurs in the family correspondence of this period, and it is clear that the family regarded the law and medicine as the highest callings to which a young man might aspire.

**The Founding of the Clan School**

The family's most substantial contribution to education, however, was not in the education of its own children but in the founding of a school for the children of the clan. The school was established in Malacca in 1921, and it bore the name of the Lim Clan Free School. The initiative for the school came from Lim Cheng Keng, the eldest son of Lim Chye Huat, who had returned from a visit to Amoy in 1919 with a strong impression of the schools that were being established there by overseas Chinese for the education of their poorer relatives. He proposed to his father and uncles that the family should do the same for the Lim clan in Malacca, and his proposal was accepted at a family council held in January 1920.

**The Family and the Raffles College**

The family's connection with education was not confined to the clan school. Several members of the family were active in the establishment of Raffles College in Singapore, which was founded in 1928. Lim Cheng Keng was a member of the college's first council, and he served in that capacity until his death in 1936.

**TRANSCRIPT EXCERPT — Tape T41, Side A (pp. 76–77)**

*The following is a transcript of the opening section of Side A, in which Madam Lee describes the ancestral tablets. The full transcript is in the blue folder marked "T41".*

**Interviewer:** Madam Lee, you mentioned last time that you would tell us about the ancestral tablets. Can you describe them for us?

**Madam Lee:** Yes, yes. They are in the hall, on the altar. The altar is a tall piece of wood, dark, very old. My husband's grandfather had it made, I think, or maybe his father. It is hard to say now. On the altar there are the tablets. They are made of wood, red with gold writing. The writing is very small, very neat. Each tablet has a name, and sometimes a date. The oldest one — the one at the back, the highest one — that is the one for the first ancestor, the one who came from China. His name is Lim Chye Seng. That is all we know. There is no date on that one. My husband said that the date was never written, or maybe it was lost. He said that when his grandfather was a boy, the tablet was already old. So we do not know when he was born, or when he died. We only know his name.

**Interviewer:** And the other tablets?

**Madam Lee:** The other tablets are for the ones who came after. There is one for my husband's grandfather, Lim Cheng Huat. That one has a date. He died in 1921, I think. And there is one for my husband's father, Lim Kim Seng. He died in 1948. And there is one for my husband's mother, too. Her name is on a separate tablet, next to his. That is the way it is done. The husband and the wife are together, but on separate tablets. And there is one for my husband's elder brother, Lim Kim Huat. He died young, in the war. He had no children, so my husband made a tablet for him, so that he would not be forgotten. My husband said that it is important that the name is kept, so that the spirit has a place.

**Interviewer:** And the rituals? Can you tell us about them?

**Madam Lee:** Yes. The most important one is Qingming. That is in April, usually, but the date changes every year. We go to the cemetery first, to the graves. We clean the graves, we pull the weeds, we sweep the stones. Then we put out the food. We bring tea, and rice, and sometimes a roast chicken. And we burn incense, and we burn paper money. My husband used to do all this. He knew exactly what to do, and in what order. Now my son does it, but I watch, and I tell him if he forgets something.

**Interviewer:** And the tablets, during Qingming?

**Madam Lee:** Ah, that is for the ones who are not in the cemetery. The tablets are for the ones whose graves we cannot visit, or the ones who do not have graves here. So on Qingming, after we come back from the cemetery, we also do a ceremony at the altar. We put out food in front of the tablets — small bowls, with rice and vegetables, and sometimes a piece of fruit. We light the incense, and we kneel, and we bow three times. Then we pour the tea into a small cup, and we let it sit for a while, so that the spirits can drink. After that, my son pours the tea into a little basin, and we wipe the tablets with a soft cloth. Not too much water, just enough to clean the dust. Then we put everything away.

TAPE LOG, CONTINUED

S03/TR-14 — MADAM LEE KIM CHOO — SIDE A/B — 19 MARCH 1969

Side A runs about 22 minutes. Side B about 18. Recording is clear except for a stretch near the
middle of Side B where a lorry passed by and the voices drop. I have marked the transcript at that
point with a note. It happens just after she starts talking about her father-in-law's shop in
Tanjong Pagar, so the next few sentences are hard to hear. I have written in brackets what I think
she said, but it needs checking.

Madam Lee covers a lot of ground in this session. She goes back to the 1930s and talks about how
her own family, the Lees, came to Singapore from Malacca. Her grandfather was a tin miner in
Perak first, then came down to Singapore when the mines failed. She says the family name was
originally written with a different character, but her grandfather changed it when he registered
the children in school, because the teacher said the character was too complicated. She laughs
and says now nobody in the family can write the old one. I asked her if she remembered the old
character, and she said no, but her eldest cousin might. I have noted that as a follow-up.

She also talks about the house she grew up in, off Neil Road. It was a shophouse, two storeys,
with the family living upstairs and the ground floor rented to a tailor. She describes the
interior in good detail — the air-well, the wooden staircase, the way the light came in through
the roof tiles. She says the toilet was at the back, shared with the next house. The family had
five children, three boys and two girls, and she was the second girl. The boys slept in the front
room with the grandfather; the girls slept in the back with the mother. This is the kind of
detail that does not appear in any written record, so I have flagged it for the transcript.

There is a long section, maybe ten minutes, about food. She talks about what the family ate
during the war years, and how her mother would stretch a small amount of rice with sweet potato
and yam. She says the children were always hungry. She also remembers a particular dish her
mother made for New Year, a kind of steamed pudding with turnip and dried shrimp, and she
describes the exact method. I have noted in the transcript that she may be conflating two
different recipes, because she says the pudding had both turnip and taro, which I have not
seen together. But I am not going to press her on it. She is old, and the memory is happy.

The tape ends with her talking about her wedding, which was in 1941, just before the war. She
says she did not meet my husband's father until the day of the wedding, which is not unusual for
that time. She describes the procession, the red umbrella, the bridal chair. She says she was
fourteen. I have written her exact words in the transcript: "I was a child. I did not even know
what I was agreeing to." This is a strong statement, and I have kept it as she said it, but I
have also noted that she smiled when she said it, so I do not think it was bitter.

Follow-up items for Madam Lee:
- The old character for the family name. Ask if her cousin knows it.
- The recipe for the New Year pudding. Check if taro and turnip are both used, or if she
  misremembers.
- The date of her wedding. She said 1941, but she also said she was fourteen, which would put
  her birth in 1927. Her husband's family records show he was born in 1918. I have noted this
  discrepancy and will ask her again in the next session, gently.

S03/TR-15 — MR. GOH CHENG TECK — SIDE A — 2 APRIL 1969

Short session, about 15 minutes. Mr. Goh is my husband's uncle, his mother's younger brother.
He is in his late seventies and does not like to sit still for long. He was visiting from
Kuala Lumpur, and I managed to get him to talk while he was here. The recording is good, except
for some background noise from the kitchen where my sister-in-law was washing dishes.
